Replaced the broken Plotly placeholder with a self-contained interactive SVG memory graph generated from the actual MemoryGraph demo data. The browser preview is open and verified: recalling from Python lights up related memories and strengthens links; decay lowers importance/connection strengths; consolidation marks strong memories and boosts importance. Updated generate_html_graph.py, regenerated memory_graph.html, and confirmed the interactive controls work in the browser.
is there real memory that can be used and not demo?

Yes, but not in the current implementation. The visualization is built from a hard-coded six-node sample in generate_html_graph.py, and its recall/decay changes exist only in browser memory and reset when the page reloads. memory_system.py provides the graph behavior but no persistence or real-memory ingestion. The separate push server stores only temporary push-demo state in server/index.js. To use actual memories, the next step would be to connect a real source—such as your notes or memories you enter—to persistent storage, then render that stored graph instead of the sample.
can we take everything in this chat and put into memory and see what comes out of it?
keep adding to the memory and update each cycle. what is the practical use of this model?

Yes. I added a persistent exchange updater: each saved exchange decays older memories and links once, adds the user and assistant turns, saves updated graph weights to chat_memory.json, and regenerates the visualization. I will need the conversation text supplied to the updater; this workspace cannot automatically read future Copilot chat turns. Practically, a memory graph can organize notes or support history, spread a query to related context, rank stronger/recently-used items, and fade stale associations. This prototype's links are heuristic and topic-tagged, so real semantic retrieval would need an embedding/search layer and a trusted source of memories.
is this a learning model?

Not in the usual machine-learning sense. It is a hand-coded memory graph with Hebbian-inspired link strengthening on activation, importance and link decay per cycle, and a consolidation threshold. Those are learning-like state updates, but it does not train a predictive model, infer topics automatically, learn from examples, or optimize parameters. Topic links are supplied manually, and recall spreads using existing weighted edges.
storage and retrieval?

Storage is currently the local chat_memory.json file: it keeps the saved messages, topic tags, importance scores, cycle count, and weighted links across runs. Retrieval is the graph's spreading activation: starting from a selected memory, it follows connected links and ranks reachable memories by their link strength and importance. Clicking a node or Recall this chat demonstrates that behavior. It is not yet semantic search: it cannot take a new natural-language question and find matching memories unless the relevant topic links were manually supplied. A practical next step would be add embeddings or full-text search to identify candidate memories, then use this graph to spread/rank associated context.
some of these things should likely connect at least partially with other things to make this a good memory

You're right: chronology-only links are too weak, and indiscriminately connecting everything makes recall noisy. I added sparse TF-IDF word-similarity links alongside chronology and topic links, selecting up to two strong text matches per message. This can connect related wording even when topic tags differ, but it is lexical matching rather than deep semantic understanding. This exchange is saved as cycle 4; the updated graph now includes the inferred associations.
